title: MV-FGAD: Multi-View Federated Graph Anomaly Detection
one_liner: Federated graph anomaly detection using multiple views and shared knowledge to catch both obvious and subtle abnormal nodes.
lead: When multiple organizations need to find abnormal nodes (fraud, defects, attacks) in their separate graphs without sharing raw data, the standard approach fails: each organization tries to spot anomalies in its own chunk of graph, but anomalies are often subtle and hidden in the structure. This paper shows that splitting the graph across organizations breaks the old neighbor-aggregation detection strategy, and introduces a method that learns a shared knowledge base about normal patterns across all organizations and uses multiple angles of view to catch weak anomalies others miss.

problem.h2: Why existing federated anomaly detection breaks
paras: Imagine multiple hospitals, each with a patient network and health records, trying to spot diseases spreading silently through connected patients. Each hospital only sees its own network chunk. The old approach says: look at each patient's neighbors and if they stand out, flag them as sick. But here is the snag: if a disease spreads slowly through the network in a way that looks almost normal (weak signal), and the hospital only sees a tiny piece of the network, the neighbors do not add up to enough evidence to raise an alarm.

Equally damaging: when you split the graph across hospitals, every organization learns its own local detector in isolation. No organization sees the full pattern of normal behavior, so no one builds a good baseline to detect subtle outliers.

callout.html: The method learns a shared knowledge base of normal patterns across all organizations and uses multiple scoring angles to catch anomalies weak and strong.

steps.b: Each site builds a local detector
steps.text: Hospital A learns patterns from its own patient network chunk.
Every hospital sends only a compressed summary (not raw data) of normal node patterns to a central server.
Central server combines all summaries into one global template of what normal looks like.
Each hospital receives the shared baseline and retrains its local detector using both its own data and this global baseline.
Each node is scored separately on several learned views; a node is flagged if it stands out in any view.

paras: The paper changes how local detectors are built: instead of training each hospital's detector in isolation, it first learns a shared knowledge base from all hospitals and uses that to guide the local detector. It also changes how a node is scored from one number to multiple numbers (one for each view), catching more types of weak anomalies.

hidden.name: How far a node sits from normal
paras: The paper's core insight is that anomalies come in two kinds: strong anomalies scream loud and obvious to any detector; weak anomalies whisper and are nearly silent. The hidden quantity is the distance from normal, usually measured in a learned space where normal nodes cluster tightly. But simply squashing the graph into one space (one view) fails: weak anomalies that are anomalous in one way may blend in when projected to a single view.

MV-FGAD measures this distance using Mahalanobis distance (a statistical measure that accounts for how spread out normal nodes are in each direction). By learning multiple separate spaces (views), each one sensitive to different kinds of weirdness, the method gives weak anomalies more chances to stand out.

heat.caption: Darker means farther from normal in Mahalanobis distance. Highlight shows anomalies that multi-view catches but single-view misses.

reads.html: A weak anomaly is a node that is only slightly unusual, barely noticeable in the full graph, but clearly odd once you zoom in on the right angle.

Mahalanobis distance accounts for correlations among features and penalizes deviations in high-variance directions less than in low-variance directions, making weak anomalies in minority directions visible.

paras: The key is federated knowledge exchange. In isolation, a hospital with only 50 patients cannot learn what true normal looks like. But if 10 hospitals pool their knowledge (without sharing raw data), normal looks like 500 patients' worth of patterns, and anomalies stand out crisply by comparison. This shared baseline is then fed back to help each local detector refit: the detector now has a much better reference model of normal, so it can confidently say a borderline node is weird because it differs from the pooled-knowledge normal in ways the isolated local normal would have tolerated as routine variation.

The second key is multi-view learning. Anomaly types vary: some nodes have weird attributes (age seems wrong for the diagnosis), others have weird network position (connected to unlikely neighbors), others have weird structural roles. A single view collapses these onto one axis and weak signals in the minority direction get lost in noise. Multiple views each tune to different anomaly types, so weak signals in each view are amplified.

stages.s: Each site has its network chunk with some nodes.
Federate: send summaries to central server.
Server merges summaries into shared normal baseline.
Broadcast baseline back; refit with shared knowledge.
Score nodes through multiple learned views.
Flag nodes that are outliers in any view.

math.words: For each view, the score of a node is the Mahalanobis distance from the mean of normal nodes, weighted by the inverse of the covariance matrix so that deviations in thick-spread directions are softer than deviations in tight directions. A node is an anomaly if its score is larger than a threshold.
symbols: the node's feature values (a list of numbers)
the average of normal nodes in view v
how much normal nodes spread in each direction in view v
the inverse; makes tight directions punish deviations more
how far x is from normal in view v
take the square root so the score stays interpretable

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine view 1 measures graph position (one number per node). Normal nodes average 50, spread is 10 (variance).
Node A has value 70. Score_1(A) = sqrt( (70-50)^2 / 100 ) = sqrt(400/100) = sqrt(4) = 2.0.
Now view 2 measures attribute weirdness. Normal average 30, spread is 5 (tighter).
Node A has value 35 in view 2. Score_2(A) = sqrt( (35-30)^2 / 25 ) = sqrt(25/25) = 1.0.
Node A: score 2.0 in view 1, score 1.0 in view 2. If threshold is 1.5, A is flagged in view 1.
A weak anomaly might score 1.2 in view 1 and 1.4 in view 2: alone both pass the threshold, but multiple views together signal it.

math.note: Mahalanobis distance lets tight directions scream loud (high penalty for small deviations) while loose directions tolerate noise, so weak signals in rare directions are amplified.

bars.h2: Single view vs. multi-view on weak anomalies

charts.title: Single view (old method)
charts.note: Single view squashes all anomaly types to one score; weak signals in minority directions vanish into noise.

charts.title: Multi-view (this paper)
charts.note: Multiple views each tune to different anomaly types, raising sensitivity to weak signals across all directions.

items.html: If the central server is slow or unreliable, the entire system stalls because all sites must wait for the shared baseline. The method works best when the central server can aggregate and broadcast quickly.

items.b: Threshold tuning across multiple views is tricky.
items.html: With one view you pick one threshold; with five views you must decide whether to flag a node if any view screams, or only if most do. The paper must choose this carefully or you get either too many false alarms or too many misses.

items.b: Views can be redundant or fail to capture all anomaly types.
items.html: If all learned views are similar (because the learning process got stuck in one local pattern), the multi-view gain vanishes. If real anomalies do not fit any of the learned views, they go invisible.

items.b: Federated knowledge exchange is non-trivial in practice.
items.html: Compressing node patterns into summaries that preserve normal behavior is an art; if the compression is lossy and destroys important variance information, the shared baseline becomes unreliable.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy federated scenario with three simulated hospitals, each with 100-node network. Insert a few obvious anomalies (high-degree outliers) and a few subtle ones (nearly-normal structure but weird attributes). Run the old single-view method and MV-FGAD. Count how many of each type of anomaly each method catches. Plot the detection rate (anomalies caught) and false-positive rate (normal nodes wrongly flagged) for both methods as you vary the threshold from strict to loose.
demo.metric_eq: detection rate = anomalies caught / total anomalies; false positive rate = normal nodes flagged / total normal nodes
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that at equal false-alarm rates, MV-FGAD catches roughly twice as many weak anomalies as the single-view baseline.
